analysis.one_liner: Creates a standalone federal agency to regulate how companies collect and use personal data.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with no cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote in the Senate Commerce Committee and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create an independent Data Protection Agency to police how companies collect, sell, and use personal information. It would require companies over a modest size threshold to submit to oversight of "high-risk" practices like facial recognition, geolocation tracking, and profiling used in hiring, credit, insurance, and housing decisions. It would also let consumers file complaints that companies must answer in writing, levy fines of up to $1 million per day for knowing violations, and put those fines into a fund that compensates people harmed by violations.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people whose personal data — browsing history, location, health, finances, biometric identifiers — is currently harvested and sold with little oversight. Anyone denied a job, credit, insurance, or housing by an opaque algorithm would gain a regulator that examines those systems, and anyone harmed by a privacy violation could receive compensation from penalties the agency collects. The bill also bans "pay-for-privacy" schemes where companies charge people extra to not be spied on, and keeps stronger state privacy laws intact [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone whose data is collected online

how_it_helps.text: Establishes an independent Data Protection Agency whose core mission is to limit the collection, disclosure, processing, and misuse of personal data by companies [S2] [S3].

Requires companies with over $25 million in revenue, that handle data on 50,000 or more people, or that sell personal data, to submit to periodic examinations and pre-approval review of high-risk practices like biometric identification, geolocation tracking, large-scale profiling, and automated decisions affecting jobs, credit, housing, and health care [S3].

Gives the agency subpoena power, allows civil penalties of up to $5,000 per day for violations, $25,000 for reckless violations, and $1 million per day for knowing violations, and routes penalty money into a Relief Fund that compensates people harmed by violations [S3].

Requires companies to respond to consumer complaints and inquiries in writing, bans pay-for-privacy and take-it-or-leave-it terms of service, and preserves the ability of state attorneys general and stronger state privacy laws to apply [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies whose business models depend on collecting and monetizing personal data: data brokers, advertising-technology firms, and large internet platforms. They would face compliance costs, examinations, and fines, and could lose revenue from selling consumer profiles. Some compliance costs would likely pass to consumers in the form of prices or fewer free ad-supported services [S3].

drawbacks.text: The $25 million revenue and 50,000-person thresholds sweep in far more than just Big Tech, pulling ordinary mid-sized businesses into a new supervisory regime with compliance costs [S3].

The bill creates a second federal regulator alongside the FTC and CFPB; while it preserves existing agencies' authority, overlapping jurisdiction over privacy enforcement could produce inconsistent rules and confusion for both companies and consumers [S3].

The definitions of personal data and high-risk practices are extremely broad, covering everything from IP addresses to inferences drawn from purchasing history, which could make it hard for businesses of any size to know in advance what is permitted [S3].
The agency's funding is an open-ended authorization of 'such sums as may be necessary,' with no spending cap [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people the upside is substantial: a dedicated regulator with real teeth over data practices that determine who gets hired, insured, and housed, plus compensation funded by violators. The real costs fall on companies that monetize personal data, and some of that expense would ripple to consumers. The main design weakness is breadth — the thresholds and definitions capture many businesses beyond the intended targets, and a new agency overlapping the FTC could mean slower, muddier enforcement in the early years.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing, a mark-up, or a floor vote, and expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the Data Protection Act of 2020 on February 13, 2020, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S1] [S5].
No other senator cosponsored the bill [S4].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no mark-up, no vote — and the bill died at the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021 [S5].

The bill would have stripped privacy rulemaking authority from the Federal Trade Commission over specified laws and moved it to the new agency, while leaving the FTC's other authorities untouched [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers, adtech firms, and large platforms that profit from collecting and selling personal information were better off, since no federal data protection regime advanced. The FTC also kept sole authority over the privacy laws it would otherwise have shared.

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.role: U.S. Senator from New York, sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Data Protection Act of 2020 and referred it to the Senate Commerce Committee.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral under Chair Roger Wicker (R-MS)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or mark-up; it sat in committee from referral until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes ever occurred and no senator of either party signed on, so the bill's fate reflects a lack of engagement from both parties rather than a recorded party split.

industries.note: Companies that derive revenue from selling personal data would face examinations, civil penalties up to $1 million per day, and a regulator empowered to restrict their core product. Their loss is the public's gain in this bill, since the data being sold is consumers' own information.

Platforms above the bill's thresholds would face ongoing supervision, mandated impact assessments for profiling and targeted advertising, and written response requirements for consumer complaints. Compliance would be costly, but codified federal standards with a single regulator could also offer more certainty than today's patchwork.

The bill transfers the FTC's rulemaking and study authority over a list of privacy laws (children's privacy, spam, do-not-call, credit reporting, and others) to the new agency, though the FTC keeps all other authorities. Consumers lose nothing directly; the shift is about bureaucratic control of privacy enforcement.
